questions.stem: A Lambda function's dependencies, including machine learning libraries, are larger than the .zip deployment package size limit. How should the developer package the function?

options.text: As several .zip files uploaded together
options.rationale: A function has one deployment package.

options.text: As a container image stored in Amazon ECR
options.rationale: Container images allow much larger function packages than .zip archives.

options.text: With the libraries listed in environment variables
options.rationale: Environment variables cannot hold libraries.

options.text: With a longer function timeout
options.rationale: Timeout does not change the package size limit.

questions.explanation: Use container images for large dependencies; use .zip and layers for smaller packages.

questions.stem: An Amazon ECS service uses rolling deployments. When a new revision's tasks keep failing health checks, the team wants the deployment to stop and return to the last working revision automatically. What should the developer enable?

options.text: A Fargate Spot capacity provider for the service's tasks
options.rationale: Spot capacity changes pricing, not deployment behavior.

options.text: A larger task memory size
options.rationale: More memory does not detect failed deployments.

options.text: The deployment circuit breaker with rollback
options.rationale: The circuit breaker detects a failing deployment and rolls back to the last completed one.

options.text: ECR tag immutability
options.rationale: Immutable tags protect images, not running deployments.

questions.explanation: ECS rolling deployments can roll back automatically with the deployment circuit breaker.

questions.stem: A team wants to run containers on Amazon ECS without provisioning, patching or scaling any EC2 instances. Which launch type should the developer specify in the service?

options.text: The EC2 launch type
options.rationale: The EC2 launch type runs tasks on instances the team manages.

options.text: An Auto Scaling group of Spot Instances
options.rationale: The team would still manage those instances.

options.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
options.rationale: Beanstalk is an application platform, not an ECS launch type.

options.text: AWS Fargate
options.rationale: Fargate runs tasks on serverless compute that AWS manages.

questions.explanation: Fargate removes server management for ECS and EKS workloads.

questions.stem: A team deploys a Lambda function with AWS SAM. New versions should receive 10 percent of traffic first, then all traffic a few minutes later, and roll back automatically if a CloudWatch alarm fires. What should the developer configure?

options.text: A canary deployment preference with the alarm listed
options.rationale: SAM's DeploymentPreference creates a CodeDeploy canary deployment that shifts traffic in two steps and watches alarms.

options.text: An all-at-once deployment preference with the alarm listed
options.rationale: All traffic moves at once, so there is no small first step.

options.text: Two Lambda layers, one for each version
options.rationale: Layers share code; they do not shift traffic.

options.text: Reserved concurrency of 10 percent on the new version
options.rationale: Concurrency limits do not route traffic between versions.

questions.explanation: Ten percent first and the rest a few minutes later is a canary pattern, and listing the alarm lets CodeDeploy roll back automatically. All-at-once is the nearest distractor, but it moves all traffic in one step.

questions.stem: A team wants to release a new version of an application alongside the current one, then move traffic over and be able to switch back immediately if problems appear. Which deployment strategy fits?

options.text: In-place rolling
options.rationale: Instances are updated in batches, so going back means redeploying.

options.text: Blue/green
options.rationale: The old environment stays in place, so traffic can be switched back quickly.

options.text: All at once
options.rationale: Every target is updated together with no previous environment to return to.

options.text: Recreate
options.rationale: The old version is removed before the new one starts.

questions.explanation: Blue/green keeps two environments, which makes rollback a traffic switch.

questions.stem: A team uses AWS CodePipeline. Each push to the main branch should start the pipeline, and a team lead must sign off before the production stage runs. Which steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action before the production stage
options.rationale: The pipeline pauses until someone approves or rejects.

options.text: Add CloudFormation drift detection to the build stage
options.rationale: Drift detection compares stacks to templates; it is not an approval.

options.text: Use a source action that starts the pipeline on each push
options.rationale: A connection-based source action detects pushes to the repository and starts the pipeline.

options.text: Schedule the pipeline to run every night with Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
options.rationale: A nightly run does not start the pipeline on each push.

options.text: Give the team lead permission to edit the buildspec file
options.rationale: Editing the build does not create an approval gate.

questions.explanation: CodePipeline orchestrates stages; approvals add a human gate between them.

questions.stem: A CloudFormation stack update must roll back automatically if an application error alarm goes into ALARM state during the update or shortly after. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Termination protection on the stack
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents stack deletion.

options.text: A DeletionPolicy of Retain on each resource
options.rationale: Retain keeps resources when they are deleted; it does not watch alarms.

options.text: Rollback triggers on the stack that monitor the alarm
options.rationale: CloudFormation watches the alarms during the update and a monitoring period, and rolls back if one fires.

options.text: Drift detection that runs automatically after each update
options.rationale: Drift detection reports manual changes; it does not roll back.

questions.explanation: Rollback triggers connect CloudWatch alarms to CloudFormation updates.

questions.stem: Before updating a production CloudFormation stack, a developer wants to see which resources will be added, changed or replaced. What should the developer create?

options.text: A stack set
options.rationale: Stack sets deploy stacks across accounts and Regions.

options.text: A drift detection report
options.rationale: Drift shows differences from the current template, not from a proposed update.

options.text: A nested stack
options.rationale: Nested stacks organize templates; they do not preview updates.

options.text: A change set
options.rationale: A change set previews the changes an update will make before you run it.

questions.explanation: The clue is previewing a proposed update: a change set lists what will be added, changed or replaced before you run it. Drift detection is the nearest distractor, but it compares resources with the current template, not with an update.

questions.stem: A network stack creates a VPC. A separate application stack in the same account and Region must use that VPC's ID without hardcoding it. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Copy the VPC ID into the application template by hand
options.rationale: Hardcoded IDs break when the network stack changes.

options.text: In the application stack, import the value with Fn::ImportValue
options.rationale: Fn::ImportValue reads a value that another stack has exported.

options.text: In the application stack, read the VPC ID with Fn::GetAtt on the network stack
options.rationale: Fn::GetAtt reads attributes of resources in the same template.

options.text: Pass the VPC ID to the application stack through a Lambda environment variable
options.rationale: Environment variables configure functions, not templates.

options.text: In the network stack, output the VPC ID with an Export name
options.rationale: An exported output can be imported by other stacks in the same account and Region.

questions.explanation: A cross-stack reference is an exported output in one stack plus Fn::ImportValue in the other. Fn::GetAtt is the nearest distractor, but it reads only resources in the same template.

questions.stem: A team wants to mark the exact commit that was released to production as version 2.3.0, so it can be found and redeployed later. What should the developer create?

options.text: A branch named release-2.3.0 created from that commit
options.rationale: A branch moves forward as new commits are added, so it does not pin one released commit.

options.text: A Git tag on that commit
options.rationale: Tags label specific commits, such as release versions.

options.text: A Lambda alias named 2.3.0
options.rationale: Aliases point to function versions, not source commits.

options.text: A pull request titled 2.3.0
options.rationale: Pull requests propose changes; they do not label a commit.

questions.explanation: A tag is a fixed label on one commit, which suits releases. A branch is the nearest distractor, but it moves as work continues on it.

questions.stem: A team wants to run the Kiro agent inside its CI/CD pipeline, without an interactive sign-in, to troubleshoot failed builds. How can the pipeline run Kiro?

options.text: Install the Kiro IDE on the build server and open it for each run
options.rationale: The IDE needs an interactive user.

options.text: Add a Kiro steering file to the buildspec
options.rationale: Steering files guide the agent; they do not run it.

options.text: Use the Kiro CLI in headless mode with API key authentication
options.rationale: Headless mode lets the CLI run in automation without an interactive session.

options.text: Store a Kiro spec in Amazon ECR
options.rationale: ECR stores container images, not Kiro specs.

questions.explanation: Headless mode runs the Kiro CLI without an interactive terminal, using an API key set in the KIRO_API_KEY environment variable, so a pipeline can use it for tasks such as code reviews and troubleshooting build failures.

questions.stem: A team deploys Lambda function versions with AWS CodeDeploy. Before any traffic shifts to a new version, a test function must call it and confirm it works, and the deployment must stop if the test fails. Where should the developer configure the test function?

options.text: As an AfterAllowTraffic hook in the AppSpec file
options.rationale: That hook runs after traffic has already moved to the new version.

options.text: As a BeforeAllowTraffic hook in the AppSpec file
options.rationale: CodeDeploy runs the hook before shifting traffic, and a failed hook stops the deployment.

options.text: As an on-failure destination on the new version
options.rationale: Destinations route asynchronous invocation results; they do not gate deployments.

options.text: As a CloudWatch alarm action on the new version's Errors metric
options.rationale: An alarm reacts to errors from live traffic, after traffic has shifted.

questions.explanation: For Lambda deployments, AppSpec hooks run validation functions before and after traffic shifts.

questions.stem: An AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployment to EC2 instances must run a smoke test script after the new version of the application has started. A failed test must fail the deployment. Which lifecycle event hook should run the script?

options.text: BeforeInstall
options.rationale: This runs before the new files are installed, so there is nothing new to test yet.

options.text: ApplicationStop
options.rationale: This runs at the start of a deployment to stop the old version of the application.

options.text: ValidateService
options.rationale: ValidateService runs last, after ApplicationStart, and is meant for checking that the deployment succeeded.

options.text: DownloadBundle
options.rationale: This event is reserved for the CodeDeploy agent and cannot run scripts.

questions.explanation: EC2 AppSpec hooks run in order: ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService.

questions.stem: An AWS CodeDeploy deployment group deploys to EC2 instances. If a CloudWatch alarm on application errors goes into ALARM during a deployment, the previous version must be redeployed automatically. What should the developer configure on the deployment group?

options.text: CloudFormation rollback triggers on the stack that holds the instances
options.rationale: Rollback triggers apply to stack updates, not to CodeDeploy application deployments.

options.text: An Amazon SNS topic that emails the team when the deployment fails
options.rationale: A notification does not roll anything back.

options.text: A larger minimum healthy hosts value for the deployment group
options.rationale: This controls how many instances stay in service during a deployment, not rollback.

options.text: The alarm, plus automatic rollback when an alarm threshold is met
options.rationale: CodeDeploy watches the listed alarms and rolls back to the last good revision when one goes into ALARM.

questions.explanation: CodeDeploy deployment groups support automatic rollback on deployment failure or on CloudWatch alarms.

questions.stem: In AWS CodePipeline, a CodeBuild action compiles an application, but the deploy action that follows receives no files to deploy. What should the developer fix?

options.text: Add an artifacts section to the buildspec that lists the output files
options.rationale: CodeBuild uploads only the files named in the artifacts section as the action's output artifact.

options.text: Give the deploy action a longer timeout
options.rationale: The deploy action has nothing to wait for; the build produced no artifact.

options.text: Add a cache section to the buildspec
options.rationale: The cache speeds up later builds; it is not passed to the next action.

options.text: Write the build output to the build container's /tmp folder
options.rationale: Files in the build container are discarded unless listed as artifacts.

questions.explanation: The buildspec artifacts section defines what a CodeBuild action hands to later pipeline actions.

questions.stem: A developer pushed a new image tag, v2, to Amazon ECR. The Amazon ECS service still runs the v1 image. The task definition refers to images by version tag. What should the developer do to deploy v2?

options.text: Restart the ECS container agent on the cluster's instances
options.rationale: The agent restart does not change which image the service's task definition names.

options.text: Register a task definition revision with the v2 image and update the service
options.rationale: A service runs a specific task definition revision; a new revision with the new image triggers a deployment.

options.text: Delete the v1 image from Amazon ECR so that ECS has to pull v2
options.rationale: Running tasks keep running, and new tasks fail because the image is gone.

options.text: Increase the service's desired count so that new tasks start
options.rationale: New tasks still use the same task definition and image.

questions.explanation: ECS deploys new images through a new task definition revision and a service update.

questions.stem: An application runs as a Kubernetes Deployment on Amazon EKS. The team wants to release a new image version without downtime, replacing pods a few at a time and only sending traffic to new pods once they are ready. What should the developer do?

options.text: Delete the existing pods so that Kubernetes recreates them with the new image
options.rationale: Deleting pods by hand causes downtime and does not change the Deployment's image.

options.text: Use the Recreate strategy so that every pod restarts at the same time
options.rationale: Recreate stops every old pod before starting new ones, which causes downtime.

options.text: Change the image with a RollingUpdate strategy and a readiness probe
options.rationale: Kubernetes replaces pods gradually and routes traffic only to pods that pass the readiness probe.

options.text: Scale the Deployment to zero, change the image, and scale it back up
options.rationale: Scaling to zero takes the application offline.

questions.explanation: Rolling updates with readiness probes give zero-downtime releases on Kubernetes.

questions.stem: A CloudFormation stack update failed, and the rollback also failed, leaving the stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. A resource that the rollback could not restore was changed outside CloudFormation. What should the developer do to make the stack usable again?

options.text: Delete the stack and every resource in it, then redeploy from scratch
options.rationale: Deleting the stack is drastic and can destroy data; continuing the rollback is the intended recovery.

options.text: Run a new stack update with the original template
options.rationale: Updates are not allowed while the stack is in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED.

options.text: Create a change set that reverts the failed update
options.rationale: Change sets cannot be run while the stack is in this state.

options.text: Fix the resource or skip it, and then continue rolling back the update
options.rationale: ContinueUpdateRollback retries the rollback, optionally skipping resources that cannot be rolled back.

questions.explanation: A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED is recovered with ContinueUpdateRollback.

questions.stem: An AWS CodePipeline pipeline deploys the same CloudFormation template to a staging stage and a production stage. Each environment needs different parameter values, such as instance sizes. How should the developer supply them?

options.text: Give each deploy action its own parameter overrides
options.rationale: Each CloudFormation deploy action can take environment-specific parameter values.

options.text: Keep a separate template for each environment with the values hardcoded
options.rationale: Duplicated templates drift apart; parameters keep one template for both.

options.text: Edit the parameter values in the console after each deployment
options.rationale: Manual edits are slow and lost on the next deployment.

options.text: Store the values as tags on the pipeline and read them in the template
options.rationale: Templates cannot read pipeline tags.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation actions in CodePipeline accept template configuration files and parameter overrides per stage.

questions.stem: A team publishes a new version of a Lambda layer that fixes a bug in a shared library. The functions that use the layer still show the bug. What is the reason?

options.text: Lambda caches layers for 24 hours after a new version is published
options.rationale: There is no such cache; functions use the version they reference.

options.text: Functions keep using the layer version they were configured with
options.rationale: Layer versions are immutable, and functions refer to a specific version.

options.text: A new layer version applies to function versions published after it
options.rationale: Function versions do not pick up new layer versions on their own either.

options.text: The new layer version must be published in every Region first
options.rationale: Layers are Regional, but the functions here are using an old version, not a missing one.

questions.explanation: Updating a layer means publishing a new version and updating each function to use it.

questions.stem: After a release, a Lambda function's new version has a bug. The team wants to be able to return to the previous version within seconds, without redeploying code. Which combination of practices will allow this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Upload the previous .zip file again and publish it as a new version
options.rationale: This works but is a redeployment, which the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Update the alias to point back to the previous version
options.rationale: Moving the alias changes which version runs, immediately, with no new deployment.

options.text: Delete the buggy version so that Lambda falls back automatically
options.rationale: Lambda does not fall back on its own when a version is deleted.

options.text: Have callers invoke the function through an alias instead of a version number
options.rationale: Callers keep the same alias ARN while the alias moves between versions.

options.text: Have callers invoke $LATEST so that they get the newest code
options.rationale: $LATEST holds the buggy code; there is nothing to switch back to.

questions.explanation: Aliases decouple callers from versions, so a rollback is just moving the alias.
